conceptTag: Run the numbers on one shop
readerTitle: The shop with full shelves and an empty bank account
caseNote: 가상 사례 (동네 철물점, IT 지원 회사) · 모든 수치는 설명용
insight: 가게 전체 재고를 한 덩어리로 보지 말고 품목별 회전 속도로 나누면, 현금이 묶인 곳과 품절로 손님을 잃는 곳이 동시에 보인다.
misconception: 재고가 많으면 품절은 없고, 현금이 부족하면 재고를 전부 줄이면 된다.

sources.text: 운영관리의 표준 개념 (재고 회전율 = 연간 매출원가 ÷ 평균 재고, 재고 일수 = 365 ÷ 회전율)

cards.title: The shop with full shelves and an empty bank account
body: Dana runs a busy hardware shop. She has $45,000 of stock on her shelves, and every month she struggles to pay suppliers on time.
Yet her screws and nails keep running out. Customers leave empty-handed. Too much stock and too little, in the same shop. Today you run the numbers for her.

image.label: Hardware shop with crowded garden aisle and an empty screw shelf
image.brief: 따뜻한 일러스트. 동네 철물점 내부. 한쪽 통로에는 먼지 쌓인 원예 공구가 가득하고, 반대쪽 나사·못 선반은 텅 비어 있음. 계산대 뒤에서 주인이 장부를 보며 고민. 실제 브랜드 로고 없음.

cards.title: Where is Dana's cash stuck?
body: Dana's three main categories, at cost, over one year:
Paint: $90,000 sold, $15,000 on the shelf on average. Garden tools: $24,000 sold, $24,000 on the shelf. Screws and nails: $60,000 sold, $6,000 on the shelf.

options.text: Paint, because it's the biggest category
options.feedback: Paint holds a lot of money, but it sells through about six times a year. Big isn't the same as stuck.

options.text: Garden tools, because they sell slowest
options.feedback: Right. This is **inventory turnover**: garden tools sell only once a year, so $24,000 sits for a full year before it comes back as cash.

options.text: Screws and nails, because she reorders them constantly
options.feedback: Frequent reorders feel like a cash drain, but this stock turns ten times a year. The money comes back fast.

cards.title: Same shop, three very different speeds.

breakdown.label: Garden tools
breakdown.detail: A full year on the shelf

cards.callout: Garden tools are a third of sales at most, yet over half of Dana's stock.
cards.softwareNote: A software company that prepays for a year of cloud capacity or licences has the same problem. Unused capacity is cash sitting on a shelf.

cards.title: The empty shelf has a price too.
body: Screws and nails bring in about $100,000 a year at shelf prices, roughly $274 a day, with 40% left after the cost of the goods.
They run out about 4 days a month. If half of those customers walk out, Dana loses about $6,600 in sales and **$2,600 in gross profit** a year. Some of them also buy their paint somewhere else.
This is the trade-off between **stockouts and overstock**. Dana has both, in different aisles.

options.text: Double the screw and nail stock to $12,000
options.feedback: It fixes the stockouts, but adds $6,000 of stock when cash is already tight. It solves one side of the stockout–overstock trade-off and makes the other worse.

options.text: Halve garden tool stock with a clearance sale and fewer reorders, and add $2,000 of screws and nails
options.feedback: Total stock drops from $45,000 to $35,000, freeing $10,000. Screws and nails still turn 7.5 times a year, and the empty shelf goes away. Turnover and stockouts both improve.

options.text: Run a 15% sale across the whole shop to raise cash
options.feedback: It raises cash fast, but gives away margin on paint and screws that were already selling well. The slow stock was the problem, not all of it.

cards.title: One yearly number can mislead.
body: Garden tools are seasonal. Measured in March, before spring, a big shelf may be exactly right. Check turnover at the same point each year, not just once.
Some slow items still earn their place. A rare part that brings a contractor in every month may sell little but anchor bigger orders.
And cut carefully. Trim slow stock too far and you just move the empty shelf to a new aisle.

cards.title: Now it's an IT support company.
body: You support 40 client offices. Your storeroom holds $30,000 of spare parts. Laptops: $20,000 on hand, $40,000 used a year. Docking stations: $8,000 on hand, $8,000 used. Cables and adapters: $2,000 on hand, $16,000 used, and they often run out, so technicians make second trips.

options.text: Hold fewer laptops and docks, order them next-day from a distributor, and keep more cables
options.feedback: Slow, expensive items move off your shelf, which raises inventory turnover. Cheap cables, where a stockout costs a whole site visit, get more room.

options.text: Stock more of everything so technicians never wait
options.feedback: No more second trips, but tens of thousands more in cash sit in the storeroom. You fix stockouts by paying for overstock.

options.text: Keep nothing and order every part when a job comes in
options.feedback: Cash is freed, but a $10 cable now delays a client for a day. Stockouts cost more than the stock you saved.

cards.softwareNote: If you sell hardware alongside software, the same split applies: keep fast, cheap items close and order slow, costly ones on demand.

cards.title: Split your stock by speed, then fix both ends.
body: One total stock number hides cash stuck in slow items and sales lost on fast ones. Run the numbers category by category.
**Try it today:** for your three biggest categories, divide a year of cost of goods sold by average stock on hand. Which one turns slowest, and which one runs out?
list: **Inventory turnover:** showed where Dana's cash was stuck
**Stockouts vs overstock:** priced the empty shelf and guided the fix
